title: Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.
summary: A lawful sale of an ingredient became unenforceable when the seller knowingly facilitated the buyer’s continuing scheme to mislabel imitation cheese as real cheese.
notes: 133 Wis. 2d 386, 395 N.W.2d 619 (Ct. App. 1986). Blossom sued on an open account for $138,306 owed for Kasson's last purchase; Kasson had bought roughly 100 times the quantity a starter use would require, and mislabeling let it charge about twice as much for the product.

sections.Parties: Blossom sold Isokappacase to Kasson, a cheese manufacturer. Blossom sued for $138,306 owed for its last shipment. Kasson relied on the parties’ involvement in misbranding as a defense.
sections.Material Facts:
Isokappacase could be used legitimately as a starter medium or in imitation-cheese production. It contained a high proportion of protein and, when added directly to cheese milk, increased yield. Kasson used it in that way while labeling the resulting product as real mozzarella or provolone rather than as an imitation with the required ingredient disclosure.

The volume mattered. Kasson bought vastly more than a legitimate starter use would explain. Blossom’s salesman knew the quantities and the economics of the operation. The manufacturer’s president had supplied technical assistance and warned that this use would not produce cheese meeting the real-cheese standards. Evidence showed that Blossom understood the mislabeling and continued supplying the large orders. Both businesses benefited economically; the improper labeling enabled a much higher selling price for Kasson’s output.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court dismissed Blossom’s contract claim as illegal and unenforceable. The Wisconsin Court of Appeals affirmed the refusal to enforce, while expressly limiting its reasoning to unenforceability on public-policy grounds rather than declaring the ingredient sale itself illegal.
sections.Issue: Did the seller’s performance of an otherwise lawful supply contract permit recovery when the seller knowingly facilitated the buyer’s improper use, and did the evidence support that degree of involvement?
sections.Holding: No recovery was allowed. The evidence supported knowledgeable facilitation, and the public policy embodied in the food-labeling rules justified nonenforcement.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished mere awareness of a buyer’s possible improper use from conduct undertaken to further that use. A seller that has substantially performed does not automatically lose payment because its buyer later violates the law. Here, sustained volume dealing, knowledge of the production process, and the economics of misbranding supported a finding that the supplier facilitated the scheme.

Using Restatement §§ 178 and 182, the court weighed the strength of the policy, the likelihood that nonenforcement would further it, the seriousness and deliberateness of the misconduct, and the direct connection between that misconduct and the claim. Accurate labeling was an identifiable legislative policy. The agreement’s ordinary appearance and the seller’s delivery did not erase its role in the continuing violation. The result left the buyer with the last shipment without a judicially enforceable payment obligation; the notes use that consequence to examine equal fault and the occasional availability of restitution despite illegality.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Blossom shows that formation and performance do not end the enforceability inquiry. A court must also consider the relationship between the requested judgment and public policies implicated by the transaction.

topics.public-policy: Knowingly facilitating misbranding supports nonenforcement even though selling the ingredient is itself lawful.
topics.governing-law: Statutory labeling policy informs a common-law decision about enforcing a private promise.
topics.restitution: The notes ask when denying contract enforcement should also prevent or permit recovery for benefits conferred.
topics.unjust-enrichment: The seller was left without payment even for goods delivered, illustrating that a party knowingly participating in an illegal scheme is denied restitution as well as contract recovery.

mnemonic.rationale: Imitation cheese made with real cheese
